title: Adding a subtitle service to the media stack, and what the first run broke
summary: A new container, built from code, that fetches subtitles for the whole library, and the four small defects its first deploy found.

stat.label: separate defects the first deploy found, each fixed in code instead of by hand

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My household watches a lot of shows and movies, and subtitles were a manual chore. The media stack already tracked every series and movie, so the missing piece was a service that looked up subtitles for each title and saved them beside the video.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A new container for Bazarr, declared in Terraform like every other guest, plus an Ansible role that installs it and keeps its version. The role also sets up the settings that matter: one English language profile as the default, two subtitle providers, and the connections to the two apps that manage the library.

The role reads the library apps' API keys from their own config on every run and stores neither. The one login the service needs lives in the secrets store, and a script that I run places it, so no session ever handles the credential.
Proxmox only lets the root account create bind mounts, so the shared media mount is a small script, the same split of work I use for other containers.

sections.heading: What the first run broke
paragraphs: Four defects stopped the first deploy, and none of them showed in a plan.

The default container template existed on only one of my nodes, so the first apply failed on the node I had chosen. A brand-new guest also carried package lists as old as its template, so a download returned not found until I refreshed them. Ansible's pip module needs a helper package on the target. And the newest Bazarr release needed one extra field on every language profile, or its sync with the library app crashed at the first episode and left nearly everything unsynced.
Each fix went back into the repository as its own small pull request, so the next guest I build does not repeat them.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: Bazarr is live. On its first pass it saw the whole library and began writing subtitle files, and Plex lists them as external tracks after a scan. The free tier of the main subtitle provider caps daily downloads, so the first pass used the day's allowance and the service throttled itself until the next day. I treated that as expected behavior and not as a fault.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: The code path was not the risky part. The risky part was everything a plan cannot see: what exists on which node, how stale a fresh image is, and how a new release changes a required field. Building the service the same way as the others turned each surprise into a one-line fix with a record of why.
